newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to legislate central bank autonomy.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to legislate central bank autonomy.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government will push through a law to enshrine central bank autonomy when the National Assembly (lower house) begins a new session on Monday, Sharif's law adviser said.

Khalid Anwer, who has ministerial status, told Reuters in an interview that a presidential ordinance passed by the previous caretaker government giving greater powers to the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) would be converted into law.
"The SBP will be given far more powers and responsibility. The board of directors will have to assume responsibility for ensuring that the government does not overspend and overborrow," Anwer said.
Giving the central bank greater muscle was a response to past perceptions of fiscal indiscipline, he said.
"Monetary policy was not being conducted in such a manner as to reduce the level of inflation, reduce deficit financing and prevent the private sector from being crowded out," Anwer said.
Other banking sector ordinances passed by the caretakers would be adopted in revised form as laws by the assembly, in which Sharif commands an overwhelming majority.
The state Pakistan Banking Council would be abolished and the legal framework of the banking sector reformed to ensure the past malpractices were reduced.
He said the government was modifying an ordinance to bring about radical changes on procedures for recovering bad debts.

Banks and financial institutions, including modarabas (Islamic mutual funds) and leasing companies, would get new powers of foreclosure. Special banking tribunals would be set up to process claims. Banks would be encouraged to clean up their balance sheets and make provision for non-performing loans.

He said banks would be discouraged from "going against the spirit of the law" by continuing to charge interest (known as mark-up in deference to the Islamic prohibition on interest) after the repayment deadline of unpaid loans.

The banking sector carries a bad debt mountain estimated at 125 billion rupees ($3.1 billion). Anwer said much of this represented loans to bankrupt companies which had closed several years ago. Accumulated interest also accounted for a major part.
Anwer blamed the present mess on the 1974 nationalisation of banks, which had led to political appointments of corrupt and inefficient bureaucrats to manage banks for a limited tenure.

Many banks had simply rescheduled bad debts, showing unpaid interest as notional profit, to make their balance sheets look good. "In the most scandalous cases, banks were actually paying income tax on non-existent profits, which greatly enhanced the dimensions of the financial losses suffered," Anwer said.

"It's the policy of the government ultimately to carry on effective privatisation, but before that we need to undertake an exercise in which we clean up the banks and arrive at a realistic appraisal of their assets and liabilities.
"Only then can we sell the banks because only then will we get the true market price, rather than the artificially low price if we sell them today," he said.
No decision had been taken on whether to set up a Resolution Trust Corporation proposed by the caretakers to assume bad debts of state-owned financial institutions, he said.
